topics.title: Kafka Architecture, Partitions & High-Throughput Commit Log
topics.summary: Deep dive into Kafka broker clustering, sequential I/O, zero-copy sendfile, and partition rebalancing.
topics.content:
## Apache Kafka Architecture & Storage Internals

### Partitioning & High-Throughput Storage
Kafka topics are divided into ordered, immutable sequences of records called **partitions**. Each partition is backed by an append-only commit log on disk.

```
Topic: payment-transactions (3 Partitions, Replication Factor = 3)

Partition 0: [Offset 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5] ──► Leader: Broker 1 (Replicas: B2, B3)
Partition 1: [Offset 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]    ──► Leader: Broker 2 (Replicas: B1, B3)
Partition 2: [Offset 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5] ──► Leader: Broker 3 (Replicas: B1, B2)
```

- **Zero-Copy Data Transfer (`sendfile` system call)**: Kafka avoids copying data into JVM application memory. Data is transferred directly from the OS Page Cache to the network NIC socket buffer, bypassing user-space CPU context switches completely!

### Consumer Group & Cooperative Rebalancing
Historically, Kafka rebalancing triggered a "Stop-The-World" Eager Rebalance, revoking all partitions from all consumers.
- Modern Kafka uses **Cooperative Sticky Assignor (`CooperativeStickyAssignor`)**: Only the specific partitions migrating to another consumer are revoked, allowing ongoing processing without pausing the entire consumer group!
topics.interviewTip: Emphasize how 'sendfile' zero-copy transfers data directly from OS page cache to network socket buffer without entering JVM user-space memory.

topics.title: Flink Event Time, Watermarks & Late Data Handling via Side Outputs
topics.summary: Master Flink time semantics: Event Time vs Processing Time, Bounded-Out-Of-Orderness watermarks, and DLQ routing with OutputTag.
topics.content:
## Flink Event Time & Late Data Handling

### Time Semantics
- **Event Time**: Timestamp embedded inside the record when event originally occurred at source (e.g. mobile app click). Immutable and deterministic.
- **Processing Time**: Wall-clock time on the TaskManager machine executing the operator. Fast, but non-deterministic on replaying stream.

### Watermarks (Tolerating Network Jitter)
A Watermark $W(t)$ is a control record asserting: *"We assume all events with timestamp $\le t$ have already arrived."*

```java
WatermarkStrategy<TransactionEvent> watermarkStrategy = WatermarkStrategy
    .<TransactionEvent>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
    .withTimestampAssigner((event, timestamp) -> event.getEventTimestamp());
```

### Late Events Handling with Side Outputs (`OutputTag`)
When an event arrives after the watermark has already advanced past its window end time:

```java
final OutputTag<TransactionEvent> lateDataTag = new OutputTag<TransactionEvent>("late-transactions"){};

SingleOutputStreamOperator<AggregatedResult> windowedStream = source
    .assignTimestampsAndWatermarks(watermarkStrategy)
    .keyBy(TransactionEvent::getUserId)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(5)))
    .sideOutputLateData(lateDataTag) // Route late events to side output!
    .aggregate(new VolumeAggregator());

// Extract late data stream and route to Kafka Dead-Letter-Queue (DLQ):
DataStream<TransactionEvent> lateStream = windowedStream.getSideOutput(lateDataTag);
lateStream.sinkTo(kafkaDlqSink);
```
topics.interviewTip: Explain why side outputs are superior to throwing late events away or setting large allowedLateness() values (which re-emits mutating window updates).

topics.title: Redis Streams vs Pub/Sub & Consumer Groups Architecture
topics.summary: Compare Redis Pub/Sub (fire-and-forget) with Redis Streams (persistent log, consumer groups, XACK, and pending entries list).
topics.content:
## Redis Streams vs Redis Pub/Sub

### Architectural Comparison

| Attribute | Redis Pub/Sub | Redis Streams (Redis 5+) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Persistence** | None (Fire-and-forget, dropped if consumer disconnected) | **Yes** (Append-only memory log on disk with RDB/AOF) |
| **Consumer Groups** | No (Every subscriber receives every message) | **Yes** (Load balances messages across consumer group) |
| **Message ACK** | None | **Yes** (`XACK` removes from Pending Entries List) |
| **History Replay** | No | **Yes** (Read historical events via offset/ID) |
| **Best For** | Chat rooms, real-time metrics push | Lightweight event queue, async task pipelines |

### Redis Streams Workflow
```
Producer ──(XADD mystream * user "Abhinav")──► Redis Stream (Log)
                                                    │
                   ┌────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┐
                   ▼                                                               ▼
        Consumer Group Worker 1                                         Consumer Group Worker 2
     (Reads via XREADGROUP)                                          (Reads via XREADGROUP)
            │                                                               │
     Processes event                                                 Processes event
            │                                                               │
     Sends XACK mystream group1 <id>                                 Sends XACK mystream group1 <id>
```

### Inspecting Crashed Workers: Pending Entries List (PEL)
If a worker crashes while processing a message, the message stays in the **Pending Entries List (PEL)**. Another worker can claim and reprocess it using `XAUTOCLAIM`:
```bash
XAUTOCLAIM mystream mygroup worker-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10
```

references.title: Redis Documentation: Introduction to Redis Streams

topics.interviewTip: Explain why Redis Pub/Sub cannot replace Kafka/RabbitMQ (unacknowledged messages are lost forever), whereas Redis Streams provides persistent consumer groups.

topics.title: Kafka Consumer Groups, Rebalancing & Partition Assignment
topics.summary: Consumer group protocol, eager vs cooperative rebalancing, partition assignors, and consumer lag monitoring strategies.
topics.content:
## Kafka Consumer Groups & Rebalancing Deep Dive

### Consumer Group Protocol
A **Consumer Group** is a set of consumers sharing the same `group.id` that collectively consume all partitions of a topic. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer at a time — this is the unit of parallelism.

```
Topic: orders (6 Partitions)

Consumer Group: order-processors
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Consumer A  ──►  Partition 0, Partition 1      │
│  Consumer B  ──►  Partition 2, Partition 3      │
│  Consumer C  ──►  Partition 4, Partition 5      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Note: max useful consumers = number of partitions
```

One consumer in the group is elected **Group Leader** by the **Group Coordinator** (a Kafka broker). The leader runs the partition assignment algorithm and sends the result back to the coordinator, which distributes assignments.

### Rebalancing: Eager vs Cooperative

#### Eager Rebalancing (Classic — Pre Kafka 2.4)
1. All consumers **stop processing** and revoke all assigned partitions.
2. All consumers rejoin the group and send `JoinGroup` requests.
3. Leader assigns partitions fresh; coordinator distributes via `SyncGroup`.
4. Consumers resume — **complete stop-the-world pause** regardless of how few partitions moved.

#### Cooperative (Incremental) Rebalancing (Kafka 2.4+)
Only partitions that *need* to move are revoked; consumers keep processing the rest:
1. **Round 1**: Consumers rejoin, leader computes new assignment and marks which partitions to revoke.
2. Affected consumers revoke only those specific partitions.
3. **Round 2**: Revoked partitions reassigned. All other consumers kept processing throughout.

```
# Enable cooperative rebalancing in consumer config
partition.assignment.strategy=org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
```

### Partition Assignors Comparison

| Assignor | Strategy | Sticky? | Cooperative? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **RangeAssignor** | Contiguous range per topic | No | No |
| **RoundRobinAssignor** | Round-robin across all partitions | No | No |
| **StickyAssignor** | Minimize movement on rebalance | Yes | No (eager) |
| **CooperativeStickyAssignor** | Sticky + incremental rebalance | Yes | **Yes** |

**RangeAssignor** can cause uneven distribution: with 3 topics of 7 partitions each, Consumer A always gets partition 0 from every topic (9 partitions) while Consumer D gets only 6.

**CooperativeStickyAssignor** is the recommended production choice — it minimizes partition movement AND avoids stop-the-world pauses.

### Consumer Lag Monitoring
Consumer lag = latest partition offset (Log End Offset) minus the consumer's committed offset.

```bash
# Check lag via kafka-consumer-groups CLI
kafka-consumer-groups.sh \
  --bootstrap-server broker:9092 \
  --group order-processors \
  --describe

# Output:
# GROUP            TOPIC    PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG
# order-processors orders   0          1540            1800            260
# order-processors orders   1          2100            2100            0
```

**JMX Metrics to Monitor:**
- `kafka.consumer:type=consumer-fetch-manager-metrics,client-id=*,attribute=records-lag-max` — max lag across all partitions
- `kafka.consumer:type=consumer-fetch-manager-metrics,attribute=records-lag-avg`

**Spring Boot Kafka Lag via Actuator:**
```yaml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,metrics
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      group-id: order-processors
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      enable-auto-commit: false
```

### Static Group Membership
Frequent restarts (e.g., rolling deploys) trigger repeated rebalances. **Static membership** prevents this:
```properties
group.instance.id=consumer-pod-1
session.timeout.ms=300000  # 5 minutes — don't trigger rebalance until timeout
```
The consumer rejoins with the same instance ID and reclaims its previous partitions without triggering a full rebalance.
topics.interviewTip: When asked about rebalancing, always distinguish eager (stop-the-world, all partitions revoked) from cooperative (incremental, only moved partitions revoked). Mention that CooperativeStickyAssignor is the modern default and dramatically reduces processing gaps in high-throughput systems.

topics.title: Schema Registry & Avro Serialization
topics.summary: Why schema evolution matters in event-driven systems, Avro binary encoding, Schema Registry compatibility modes, and Spring Boot integration.
topics.content:
## Schema Registry & Avro Serialization

### Why Schema Evolution Matters
In event-driven architectures, producers and consumers are **decoupled** — they deploy independently. Without a contract, a producer adding a new field breaks consumers expecting the old schema, and a producer removing a field breaks consumers that depend on it.

**Schema Registry** solves this by:
1. Storing versioned schemas centrally (Confluent Schema Registry, AWS Glue, Apicurio)
2. Enforcing compatibility rules before a new schema version is registered
3. Embedding only a schema ID (4 bytes) in every Kafka message instead of the full schema

```
Kafka Message Wire Format (with Schema Registry):
┌─────┬────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ 0x0 │ Schema ID  │  Avro Binary Payload          │
│(1B) │  (4 bytes) │  (compact, no field names)    │
└─────┴────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘
```

### Apache Avro: Schema Definition

```json
{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "PaymentEvent",
  "namespace": "com.example.payments",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "paymentId", "type": "string"},
    {"name": "amount",    "type": "double"},
    {"name": "currency",  "type": "string"},
    {"name": "userId",    "type": "string"},
    {"name": "metadata",  "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}
  ]
}
```

**Avro advantages over JSON:**
- Binary encoding (3-10x smaller than JSON)
- No field names in payload — schema stored separately
- Strong typing with null safety via union types
- Native support for schema evolution

### Compatibility Modes

| Mode | New Schema Can... | Old Consumers Can Read New? | New Consumers Can Read Old? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **BACKWARD** | Add optional fields, remove fields | Yes (with defaults) | No guarantee |
| **FORWARD** | Add fields, remove optional fields | No guarantee | Yes |
| **FULL** | Only add optional fields (with defaults) | Yes | Yes |
| **NONE** | Anything | Not enforced | Not enforced |

**Production recommendation**: Use **FULL** or **BACKWARD** compatibility. Always add new fields with defaults (`"default": null`).

### Schema Registry REST API

```bash
# Register a new schema version
curl -X POST http://schema-registry:8081/subjects/payments-value/versions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json" \
  -d '{"schema": "{\"type\":\"record\",\"name\":\"PaymentEvent\",...}"}'

# Check compatibility before deploying
curl -X POST http://schema-registry:8081/compatibility/subjects/payments-value/versions/latest \
  -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json" \
  -d '{"schema": "...new schema..."}'
# Response: {"is_compatible": true}

# List all versions
curl http://schema-registry:8081/subjects/payments-value/versions
```

### Spring Boot Configuration

```yaml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroSerializer
    consumer:
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroDeserializer
    properties:
      schema.registry.url: http://schema-registry:8081
      specific.avro.reader: true  # Deserialize to generated Java class, not GenericRecord
      auto.register.schemas: false  # Never auto-register in production!
```

### Protobuf Alternative
Google Protobuf is another binary serialization format with Schema Registry support:
- **Avro**: Simpler, better Hadoop/Spark ecosystem support, schema stored in registry
- **Protobuf**: Better language support, field-number-based (no name coupling), gRPC native
- **JSON Schema**: Human-readable but verbose, no binary encoding — avoid for high-throughput Kafka
topics.interviewTip: Always explain the wire format: magic byte (0x0) + 4-byte schema ID + Avro binary. This shows you understand the actual mechanics, not just the concept. Also mention that 'specific.avro.reader: true' is essential — without it you get GenericRecord objects that require manual field access.

topics.title: Kafka Connect & CDC with Debezium
topics.summary: Kafka Connect source and sink connectors, Debezium CDC from database WAL logs, the Outbox Pattern, and Single Message Transforms.
topics.content:
## Kafka Connect & Change Data Capture with Debezium

### Kafka Connect Architecture
Kafka Connect is a scalable, fault-tolerant framework for streaming data between Kafka and external systems without writing custom producer/consumer code.

```
External System                 Kafka Connect                    Kafka

  MySQL DB    ──► Source Connector (Debezium) ──►  Topic: dbserver.inventory.orders
  PostgreSQL  ──► Source Connector (Debezium) ──►  Topic: dbserver.public.payments

  Kafka Topic ──► Sink Connector (JDBC)       ──►  PostgreSQL (reporting DB)
  Kafka Topic ──► Sink Connector (S3)         ──►  AWS S3 (data lake)
  Kafka Topic ──► Sink Connector (Elasticsearch) ► Elasticsearch (search index)
```

### Debezium: Change Data Capture from Database WAL
Debezium reads the database **Write-Ahead Log (WAL)** (called binary log in MySQL, WAL in PostgreSQL) at the database level — not by polling the application tables. This captures every INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE as a structured Kafka event.

**Debezium MySQL Connector Configuration:**
```json
{
  "name": "mysql-orders-connector",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector",
    "database.hostname": "mysql-host",
    "database.port": "3306",
    "database.user": "debezium",
    "database.password": "${file:/opt/secrets.properties:db.password}",
    "database.server.id": "184054",
    "database.server.name": "dbserver1",
    "database.include.list": "inventory",
    "table.include.list": "inventory.orders,inventory.products",
    "database.history.kafka.bootstrap.servers": "kafka:9092",
    "database.history.kafka.topic": "schema-changes.inventory",
    "transforms": "unwrap",
    "transforms.unwrap.type": "io.debezium.transforms.ExtractNewRecordState"
  }
}
```

### Debezium Event Structure

```json
{
  "before": {"id": 101, "status": "PENDING", "amount": 99.99},
  "after":  {"id": 101, "status": "PAID",    "amount": 99.99},
  "source": {
    "db": "inventory",
    "table": "orders",
    "ts_ms": 1698944400000,
    "pos": 12345
  },
  "op": "u",
  "ts_ms": 1698944400500
}
```

`op` values: `c` = create, `u` = update, `d` = delete, `r` = read (snapshot)

### The Outbox Pattern with Debezium
Avoids dual-write inconsistency: instead of writing to DB AND publishing to Kafka (two-phase problem), write only to an **outbox table** in the same DB transaction. Debezium then captures from the outbox table:

```sql
-- Application writes atomically in ONE DB transaction:
INSERT INTO orders (id, amount, status) VALUES (101, 99.99, 'PENDING');
INSERT INTO outbox_events (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, type, payload)
  VALUES ('Order', 101, 'OrderCreated', '{"orderId":101,"amount":99.99}');
COMMIT;
-- Debezium picks up outbox_events and publishes to Kafka
```

### Single Message Transforms (SMT)
SMTs transform individual records in-flight without writing custom code:

```json
"transforms": "route,extractKey",
"transforms.route.type": "org.apache.kafka.connect.transforms.ReplaceField$Value",
"transforms.extractKey.type": "org.apache.kafka.connect.transforms.ExtractField$Key",
"transforms.extractKey.field": "order_id"
```

Common SMTs: `ReplaceField`, `MaskField`, `ExtractField`, `InsertField`, `TimestampConverter`, `Filter`

### Managing Connectors via REST API

```bash
# Deploy connector
curl -X POST http://connect:8083/connectors \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @mysql-connector-config.json

# Check status
curl http://connect:8083/connectors/mysql-orders-connector/status

# Restart failed task
curl -X POST http://connect:8083/connectors/mysql-orders-connector/tasks/0/restart
```
topics.interviewTip: Explain why CDC via WAL (Debezium) is superior to polling: WAL captures deletes (impossible with pure polling), has zero impact on application query load, captures every intermediate state change, and is transactionally consistent. Also explain the Outbox Pattern as the canonical solution to dual-write problems.

topics.title: Flink SQL & Table API: Streaming Queries & Windowed Aggregations
topics.summary: Flink SQL DDL for Kafka connectors, tumbling window aggregations, MATCH_RECOGNIZE for CEP in SQL, temporal joins, and when to use DataStream API.
topics.content:
## Flink SQL & Table API

### Why Flink SQL?
Flink SQL brings the familiar SQL interface to streaming data. It compiles to the same optimized DataStream API underneath but dramatically reduces boilerplate and enables non-Java teams to write streaming queries.

### Defining a Kafka Source Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    transaction_id  STRING,
    user_id         STRING,
    amount          DOUBLE,
    status          STRING,
    event_time      TIMESTAMP(3),
    WATERMARK FOR event_time AS event_time - INTERVAL '10' SECOND
) WITH (
    'connector' = 'kafka',
    'topic'     = 'payments',
    'properties.bootstrap.servers' = 'kafka:9092',
    'properties.group.id'  = 'flink-sql-consumer',
    'format'    = 'avro-confluent',
    'avro-confluent.schema-registry.url' = 'http://schema-registry:8081',
    'scan.startup.mode' = 'earliest-offset'
);

-- Kafka Sink Table
CREATE TABLE fraud_alerts (
    user_id     STRING,
    alert_time  TIMESTAMP(3),
    fail_count  BIGINT
) WITH (
    'connector' = 'kafka',
    'topic'     = 'fraud-alerts',
    'format'    = 'json'
);
```

### Tumbling Window Aggregation

```sql
-- Count failures per user per 5-minute tumbling window
INSERT INTO fraud_alerts
SELECT
    user_id,
    TUMBLE_END(event_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE) AS alert_time,
    COUNT(*) AS fail_count
FROM transactions
WHERE status = 'FAILED'
GROUP BY
    user_id,
    TUMBLE(event_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE)
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
```

### Window Types in Flink SQL

| Window | SQL Function | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Tumbling | `TUMBLE(time_col, INTERVAL)` | Fixed-size, non-overlapping windows |
| Sliding (Hop) | `HOP(time_col, slide, size)` | Overlapping windows, events appear in multiple windows |
| Session | `SESSION(time_col, gap)` | Dynamic gap-based windows, closes after inactivity |
| Cumulative | `CUMULATE(time_col, step, max)` | Growing windows that reset at max size |

### MATCH_RECOGNIZE: CEP in SQL

```sql
-- Detect: login succeeded followed by 3+ failed transactions within 10 minutes
SELECT *
FROM transactions
MATCH_RECOGNIZE (
    PARTITION BY user_id
    ORDER BY event_time
    MEASURES
        FIRST(FAIL.event_time) AS first_fail_time,
        LAST(FAIL.event_time)  AS last_fail_time,
        COUNT(FAIL.*)          AS fail_count
    ONE ROW PER MATCH
    AFTER MATCH SKIP PAST LAST ROW
    PATTERN (FAIL{3,} ) WITHIN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
    DEFINE
        FAIL AS status = 'FAILED'
);
```

### Temporal Join: Lookup Table (Slowly Changing Dimension)

```sql
-- Join each transaction with the exchange rate valid at event time
CREATE TABLE exchange_rates (
    currency    STRING,
    rate        DOUBLE,
    valid_time  TIMESTAMP(3),
    PRIMARY KEY (currency) NOT ENFORCED
) WITH (
    'connector' = 'jdbc',
    'url' = 'jdbc:postgresql://db/rates',
    'table-name' = 'exchange_rates',
    'lookup.cache.max-rows' = '1000',
    'lookup.cache.ttl' = '60s'
);

SELECT
    t.transaction_id,
    t.amount * r.rate AS amount_usd
FROM transactions t
JOIN exchange_rates FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF t.event_time AS r
    ON t.currency = r.currency;
```

### Table API (Java/Scala)

```java
StreamTableEnvironment tEnv = StreamTableEnvironment.create(env);

Table transactions = tEnv.from("transactions");

Table failureCounts = transactions
    .filter($"status".isEqual("FAILED"))
    .window(Tumble.over(lit(5).minutes()).on($"event_time").as("w"))
    .groupBy($"user_id", $"w")
    .select($"user_id", $"w".end().as("window_end"), $"status".count().as("fail_count"))
    .filter($"fail_count".isGreaterOrEqual(3));

// Convert back to DataStream for CEP or custom sinks
DataStream<Row> resultStream = tEnv.toDataStream(failureCounts);
```

### Flink SQL vs Table API vs DataStream API

| Layer | Best For |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Flink SQL** | Ad-hoc queries, analytics teams, simple ETL pipelines |
| **Table API** | Programmatic query building with type safety in Java/Python |
| **DataStream API** | Custom operators, CEP, async I/O, full control over state |

Flink SQL and Table API compile to the same Blink planner underneath — choose based on team familiarity.
topics.interviewTip: When asked about Flink SQL vs DataStream, explain that SQL is a higher abstraction that compiles to DataStream internally. Use SQL for standard aggregations and joins; drop to DataStream for custom state management, CEP, async I/O, or when you need ProcessFunction-level control. Mention MATCH_RECOGNIZE as the SQL equivalent of FlinkCEP.

topics.title: Flink Backpressure, Parallelism & Performance Tuning
topics.summary: Credit-based flow control, detecting and resolving backpressure, parallelism tuning, async I/O, state TTL, and key skew detection.
topics.content:
## Flink Backpressure, Parallelism & Performance Tuning

### Credit-Based Flow Control (Network Backpressure)
Flink uses a **credit-based** mechanism at the network layer between TaskManagers:

```
Upstream Operator           Network Buffer           Downstream Operator
     │                                                     │
     │  ◄── Credits ("I can accept N buffers") ──────────  │
     │                                                     │
     │  ──── Data (consumes credit) ────────────────────►  │
     │                                                     │
     │  (If downstream overwhelmed, credits = 0 → upstream │
     │   stops emitting → backpressure propagates up)      │
```

Backpressure propagates **upstream** through the pipeline naturally — no explicit signaling needed. Source operators slow down (e.g., Kafka consumer stops polling) when downstream is saturated.

### Detecting Backpressure via Flink UI

1. Open Flink Dashboard → Job → Operator graph
2. Each operator shows **Backpressure Status**:
   - `OK` (green): < 10% time blocked
   - `LOW` (yellow): 10–50% time blocked
   - `HIGH` (red): > 50% time blocked
3. The **bottleneck operator** is the one showing HIGH backpressure with an upstream OK neighbor.

**Key metrics:**
```
taskmanager.job.task.isBackPressured          # Boolean flag
taskmanager.job.task.backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond  # Milliseconds per second blocked
taskmanager.job.task.busyTimeMsPerSecond      # Busy time (complement of idle)
```

### Root Causes & Fixes

#### 1. Insufficient Parallelism
```java
// Set per-operator parallelism
stream
    .keyBy(Event::getUserId)
    .process(new ExpensiveProcessor())
    .setParallelism(16)   // Scale up bottleneck operator
    .sinkTo(kafkaSink)
    .setParallelism(8);

// Global default parallelism
env.setParallelism(8);
```

#### 2. Slow State Access (RocksDB)
RocksDB reads involve deserialization. Optimize:
```yaml
# flink-conf.yaml
state.backend: rocksdb
state.backend.rocksdb.block.cache-size: 256mb  # Increase block cache
state.backend.rocksdb.writebuffer.size: 64mb
state.backend.rocksdb.writebuffer.count: 3
# Use bloom filters to reduce unnecessary disk reads
state.backend.rocksdb.bloom-filter.enabled: true
```

#### 3. Async I/O for External Lookups
Blocking synchronous external calls (DB, REST API) inside operators kills throughput. Use **AsyncFunction**:

```java
public class AsyncEnrichmentFunction
    extends RichAsyncFunction<Transaction, EnrichedTransaction> {

    private AsyncHttpClient httpClient;

    @Override
    public void open(Configuration parameters) {
        httpClient = Dsl.asyncHttpClient();
    }

    @Override
    public void asyncInvoke(Transaction tx,
                            ResultFuture<EnrichedTransaction> resultFuture) {
        // Non-blocking HTTP call — thousands can be in-flight simultaneously
        httpClient.prepareGet("http://user-service/" + tx.getUserId())
            .execute(new AsyncCompletionHandler<Response>() {
                @Override
                public Response onCompleted(Response response) {
                    UserInfo user = parseResponse(response);
                    resultFuture.complete(Collections.singleton(
                        new EnrichedTransaction(tx, user)
                    ));
                    return response;
                }
            });
    }
}

// Apply with capacity limit (max in-flight requests)
DataStream<EnrichedTransaction> enriched = AsyncDataStream
    .unorderedWait(transactions, new AsyncEnrichmentFunction(),
        5, TimeUnit.SECONDS,   // timeout per request
        1000);                 // max concurrent requests
```

#### 4. State TTL to Control Size
```java
StateTtlConfig ttlConfig = StateTtlConfig
    .newBuilder(Time.hours(2))  // Expire state after 2 hours of inactivity
    .setUpdateType(StateTtlConfig.UpdateType.OnReadAndWrite)
    .setStateVisibility(StateTtlConfig.StateVisibility.NeverReturnExpired)
    .cleanupInRocksdbCompactFilter(1000)  // Check every 1000 state accesses
    .build();
```

### Key Skew Detection & Resolution
Key skew occurs when certain keys receive disproportionately more data (e.g., a single popular user ID).

```java
// Detect: check TaskManager CPU/memory in Flink UI — skewed keys land on same slot
// Resolution 1: Salt the key (pre-aggregation)
stream
    .map(e -> Tuple2.of(e.getUserId() + "_" + (e.hashCode() % 8), e))
    .keyBy(t -> t.f0)
    .process(new SaltedPartialAggregator())  // Aggregate per salt bucket
    .keyBy(partial -> partial.userId)        // Re-key to merge
    .process(new MergeAggregator());         // Final merge

// Resolution 2: Use broadcast state for hot keys
// Resolution 3: Filter hot keys to a separate high-parallelism pipeline
```

### Checkpoint Tuning for High Throughput
```yaml
execution.checkpointing.interval: 60000        # Checkpoint every 60s
execution.checkpointing.timeout: 120000        # Fail if checkpoint > 2min
execution.checkpointing.mode: EXACTLY_ONCE
execution.checkpointing.unaligned: true        # Unaligned checkpoints for high backpressure
taskmanager.network.memory.fraction: 0.15      # More memory for network buffers
```
topics.interviewTip: When asked about performance issues, follow this diagnostic flow: (1) Check Flink UI for backpressure status to identify bottleneck operator, (2) Check if it's CPU-bound (parallelism), I/O-bound (async I/O or state backend tuning), or data-skew-bound (key distribution), then apply targeted fix. Jumping straight to 'increase parallelism' without diagnosis is a red flag.

topics.title: Spark vs Flink: Architecture & When to Use What
topics.summary: Architectural differences between Spark (micro-batch) and Flink (true streaming), Catalyst optimizer, and decision framework for choosing each.
topics.content:
## Spark vs Flink: Architecture & When to Use Each

### Core Architectural Difference

```
Apache Spark Structured Streaming:

Infinite Stream ──► [Micro-batch at interval T] ──► Spark SQL Engine ──► Output
                         │
                    Treats each micro-batch as a small batch DataFrame query
                    Latency: seconds (trigger interval)
                    Processing: batch-optimized Catalyst + Tungsten

Apache Flink:

Infinite Stream ──► [Record-by-Record / Mini-batch] ──► Streaming Engine ──► Output
                         │
                    True streaming — processes each event as it arrives
                    Latency: milliseconds
                    State: local RocksDB, incrementally checkpointed
```

### Spark Architecture

| Component | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Catalyst Optimizer** | SQL query plan optimizer — rule-based + cost-based — produces optimized physical plan |
| **Tungsten Engine** | Off-heap binary memory format + LLVM-style code generation for CPU efficiency |
| **Structured Streaming** | Micro-batch streaming built on DataFrame API — same code for batch & stream |
| **MLlib** | Distributed ML library — Ridge/Lasso, GBT, k-means, ALS — mature ecosystem |
| **Delta Lake** | ACID transactions on data lake — time travel, schema enforcement |

### Flink Architecture

| Component | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **JobManager** | Master node — schedules tasks, coordinates checkpoints, manages recovery |
| **TaskManager** | Worker node — executes operator subtasks in slots |
| **State Backends** | HashMapStateBackend (in-memory) or RocksDB (disk-based, TB-scale) |
| **Event Time** | Native watermark-based event time semantics — deterministic replays |
| **CEP Library** | Complex Event Processing — pattern detection across event streams |

### Side-by-Side Comparison

| Dimension | Apache Spark | Apache Flink |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Processing Model** | Micro-batch (Structured Streaming) | True event-by-event streaming |
| **Latency** | Seconds (100ms minimum with trigger Once) | Milliseconds |
| **State Management** | Limited (stateful ops via mapGroupsWithState) | First-class (rich keyed state, TTL, RocksDB) |
| **Exactly-Once** | Yes (via WAL + idempotent sinks) | Yes (via checkpointing + transactional sinks) |
| **Batch Processing** | Mature, best-in-class (Catalyst + Tungsten) | Supported but less mature than Spark |
| **ML Ecosystem** | MLlib — extensive, production-ready | FlinkML — limited; usually delegate to Spark |
| **SQL Support** | Spark SQL — very mature, wide adoption | Flink SQL — strong but less ecosystem tools |
| **CEP** | Not native (need external libs) | Native FlinkCEP library |
| **Backpressure** | Manual trigger management | Automatic credit-based flow control |
| **Operational Complexity** | Lower (familiar SQL, Python API) | Higher (state backend tuning, watermarks) |

### Decision Framework

```
                    Is latency requirement < 1 second?
                           │
              ┌────────────┴────────────┐
             YES                       NO
              │                         │
           USE FLINK                Do you need ML at scale?
              │                         │
         Also use Flink if:      ┌──────┴──────┐
         - CEP pattern detection  YES          NO
         - Complex stateful ops   │            │
         - True event-time        MLlib     Spark Structured
           semantics needed      (Spark)     Streaming or
                                            Spark Batch
```

### Common Use Cases

**Spark wins:**
- Large-scale batch ETL jobs (petabyte-scale historical processing)
- Machine learning training pipelines
- Interactive SQL analytics (Spark SQL + Databricks)
- Teams already invested in PySpark/Scala Spark
- Delta Lake / Lakehouse architecture

**Flink wins:**
- Real-time fraud detection (millisecond response required)
- Real-time dashboards and alerting
- Complex event pattern matching (CEP)
- High-volume event enrichment with external lookups
- Applications requiring true event-time semantics and deterministic reprocessing

### Unified Architecture: Flink for Streaming, Spark for Batch

```
Kafka ──► Flink (real-time features, alerts, serving) ──► Redis/DB
  │
  └──► S3 / Delta Lake ──► Spark (batch ML training, BI reports) ──► Model Store / BI
```

Many production architectures use **both**: Flink handles the real-time serving path, Spark handles the batch/ML path. They share the same data lake (S3 + Delta/Iceberg) as the integration layer.
topics.interviewTip: Don't position Spark and Flink as competitors — they complement each other. Show you understand that Spark's micro-batch model is a deliberate design choice that enables Catalyst query optimization and simplicity, while Flink's true streaming enables millisecond latency at the cost of more operational complexity. Mention that most large companies use both.

topics.title: Data Pipeline Design: Lambda vs Kappa Architecture
topics.summary: Lambda architecture trade-offs (batch + speed + serving layers) vs Kappa's streaming-only approach, and when each is justified.
topics.content:
## Lambda vs Kappa Architecture

### Lambda Architecture (Nathan Marz, 2011)
Designed to handle massive data by splitting computation across two paths:

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
Data Source ────────►   Batch Layer (Spark on HDFS/S3)        │
    │               │   - Reprocesses ALL historical data      │
    │               │   - High latency (hours), high accuracy  │
    │               │   - Generates batch views                │
    │               └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
    │                              │ Batch views
    │               ┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
    └──────────────►│  Speed Layer (Flink/Kafka Streams)       │
                    │   - Processes ONLY recent data           │
                    │   - Low latency (ms-seconds)             │
                    │   - Generates real-time views            │
                    └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                                   │ Real-time views
                    ┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
                    │  Serving Layer (Cassandra, Redis, HBase) │
                    │   - Merges batch + real-time views        │
                    │   - Answers queries                      │
                    └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Lambda Architecture: Layers Explained

**Batch Layer:**
- Stores the complete, immutable master dataset (all historical events)
- Periodically reprocesses everything from scratch to generate accurate batch views
- Technology: Spark on S3/HDFS, Hive, Presto
- Latency: Hours to days

**Speed Layer:**
- Processes only the most recent data not yet in batch views
- Provides low-latency approximate results
- Technology: Flink, Kafka Streams, Storm
- Latency: Milliseconds to seconds

**Serving Layer:**
- Merges batch views + real-time views to answer queries
- Technology: Apache Druid, Cassandra, Redis, HBase

### Lambda Architecture Problems

1. **Two codebases**: Batch logic in Spark SQL must be replicated in Flink/Kafka Streams. Schema changes, bug fixes, and new features must be implemented twice — divergence is inevitable.
2. **Operational complexity**: Two completely different technology stacks to deploy, monitor, and tune.
3. **Serving layer merge logic**: Complex query-time merging of batch and real-time views.
4. **Reprocessing friction**: Historical reprocessing in Spark cannot be hot-swapped with the real-time path.

### Kappa Architecture (Jay Kreps, 2014)
Simplification: **everything is a stream**. Eliminate the batch layer entirely.

```
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
Data Source ───────► Kafka (Immutable, Long-Retention Event Log)    │
                    │  Retention: 90 days or unlimited (tiered)    │
                    └───────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                                        │
                    ┌───────────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
                    │  Stream Processor (Flink / Kafka Streams)    │
                    │   - Real-time processing for serving          │
                    │   - Reprocessing: deploy new version,         │
                    │     replay from beginning of Kafka log         │
                    └───────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                                        │
                    ┌───────────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
                    │  Serving Layer (Redis, Cassandra, Postgres)   │
                    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Kappa: Reprocessing Strategy
The key insight: Kafka's immutable log IS the batch layer. To reprocess:
1. Deploy new version of the Flink job with a **new consumer group** (and new output topic)
2. Set `auto.offset.reset=earliest` — consume from beginning of Kafka log
3. Once new job catches up to current time, switch serving layer to new output
4. Decommission old job

```bash
# Flink Kappa reprocessing: replay from beginning
flink run \
  -p 16 \
  -c com.example.PaymentAggregatorV2 \
  payment-aggregator-2.jar \
  --kafka.group.id=payment-aggregator-v2 \
  --kafka.auto.offset.reset=earliest \
  --output.topic=payment-aggregations-v2
```

### Lambda vs Kappa Decision Framework

| Factor | Lambda | Kappa |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Team Size** | Large teams, separate batch/streaming expertise | Smaller teams, single streaming codebase |
| **Latency** | Mixed: batch = hours, speed = ms | Uniformly low (ms to seconds) |
| **Reprocessing** | Spark batch job — mature, fast | Kafka replay — requires long retention |
| **ML Training** | Natural (batch layer = training data) | Possible but awkward (stream to S3 first) |
| **Data Volume** | Handles petabytes in batch efficiently | Kafka retention cost for very old data |
| **Correctness** | Batch layer always corrects speed layer errors | One pipeline = one place to fix bugs |

### When Lambda Is Still Justified
1. **ML training requires batch access**: Training models on 2 years of historical data — Spark batch on S3 is more efficient than Kafka replay.
2. **Regulatory reprocessing**: Compliance requires reprocessing 5+ years of data — Kafka long-term retention is expensive.
3. **Complex batch-only computations**: Graph algorithms, iterative ML — don't fit the streaming model.
4. **Legacy constraints**: Existing Spark infrastructure that's expensive to migrate.

### Log-Centric Architecture Principle
Both Lambda and Kappa share the same foundation: treat the **event log as the source of truth**. Databases, caches, and serving layers are just **materialized views** of the log that can be rebuilt at any time.

```
Kafka (Source of Truth)
    │
    ├──► Flink ──► Redis (Real-time serving cache)
    ├──► Flink ──► PostgreSQL (OLTP materialized view)
    ├──► Kafka Connect S3 Sink ──► S3 / Delta Lake (Analytics)
    └──► Elasticsearch Connector ──► Elasticsearch (Search index)
```

This mindset enables fearless migrations: if a serving store becomes corrupted or needs schema changes, you rebuild it from the Kafka log rather than attempting complex migrations.
topics.interviewTip: Show architectural maturity by pointing out Lambda's biggest failure mode: the two-codebase problem. Business logic implemented differently in Spark and Flink will diverge over time — this is not a discipline problem, it's an architectural inevitability. Kappa's single-codebase approach eliminates this entire class of bugs. Then explain when Lambda is still justified (ML training on years of data, petabyte-scale batch with mature Spark infrastructure).
